drugB: Calcium-containing IV solutions (gluconate, chloride, Ringer's lactate, Hartmann's, TPN with calcium)
oneLiner: DEATHS reported in neonates: ceftriaxone + Ca → ceftriaxone-calcium crystalline precipitate in lung/kidney → fatal embolic disease. FDA black-box. Do not co-administer; separate lines, ≥ 48 h gap in neonates.
notes: Neonates (≤ 28 days): ceftriaxone is CONTRAINDICATED with any calcium-containing IV solution or product, even via separate lines and at different times, due to fatal crystalline precipitate cases reported in pulmonary and renal tissue at post-mortem. Patients > 28 days: ceftriaxone and Ca-containing solutions may be given sequentially via the same line ONLY if the line is thoroughly flushed with a compatible fluid (NS or D5W) between infusions. Never mix in the same line / bag / syringe at any age. Avoid Ringer's lactate as the dilution / flush fluid for ceftriaxone in any patient.
alternative: Use cefotaxime (no calcium incompatibility) for neonatal sepsis. Adults: separate lines, NS flush.

references.label: FDA Safety Communication. Information for Healthcare Professionals: Ceftriaxone (marketed as Rocephin and generics). 2009.
Bradley JS et al. Intravenous ceftriaxone and calcium in the neonate: assessing the risk for cardiopulmonary adverse events. Pediatrics 2009;123:e609-13.

oneLiner: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose solutions — use NORMAL SALINE only, with an in-line 0.22 micron filter. Infusion rate ≤ 50 mg/min (adult); ≤ 1 mg/kg/min (paediatric, max 50 mg/min).
notes: Phenytoin parenteral is a highly alkaline solution (pH 12) in propylene glycol vehicle. In any dextrose-containing fluid, the pH drops and phenytoin precipitates as fine crystals — often not visually obvious before the line embolises or the drug becomes subtherapeutic. Use 0.9% NaCl (NS) only. Infuse via a dedicated large-bore peripheral or central line, with an in-line 0.22-0.45 micron filter to catch micro-precipitate. Maximum infusion rate 50 mg/min in adults; reduce to 25 mg/min in elderly / cardiovascular disease (hypotension, arrhythmia at higher rates). Pediatric: 1 mg/kg/min, max 50 mg/min. Fosphenytoin (a water-soluble pro-drug) is compatible with dextrose AND saline AND can run faster (150 mg PE/min adult).
alternative: Use fosphenytoin where available (compatible with any standard fluid). For phenytoin: dilute in NS only, use filter, dedicated line.

references.label: ASHP Therapeutic Position Statement on the use of fosphenytoin. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1999.
BNF / Phenytoin sodium injection SmPC.

oneLiner: Amiodarone precipitates in saline. Dilute in DEXTROSE 5% (D5W) only. Concentrations > 2 mg/mL via central line (peripheral vein → phlebitis).
notes: Amiodarone HCl injection is poorly soluble in 0.9% NaCl — precipitates as fine crystals visible within minutes. Always dilute in D5W. Concentrations ≤ 2 mg/mL may be given peripherally (still high phlebitis risk); > 2 mg/mL MUST be central. Use a non-PVC infusion set if available (amiodarone leaches plasticisers from PVC, and adsorbs to in-line filters > 0.22 micron significantly). In-line 0.22 micron filter is RECOMMENDED to trap micro-particulate.
alternative: If central access is unavailable for prolonged infusion: switch to oral loading when haemodynamically tolerated.

references.label: Cordarone IV (amiodarone HCl) — manufacturer prescribing information.
ASHP King Guide to Parenteral Admixtures — amiodarone.

oneLiner: Propofol is a 10% lipid emulsion — destabilises with many co-administered drugs (visible oiling, droplet enlargement). Run dedicated line; very few drugs are confirmed Y-site compatible.
notes: Propofol's lipid vehicle (Intralipid-like emulsion) is destabilised by acidic drugs, divalent cations, and most antibiotics — leading to fat globule coalescence, lipid oiling and embolism risk. Established Y-site compatible drugs (small Trissel's-confirmed list): fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil, midazolam (most studies), ketamine, dexmedetomidine, ondansetron, lorazepam (some studies), morphine, hydromorphone, naloxone, remifentanil. INCOMPATIBLE at Y-site (visible incompatibility): bretylium, calcium chloride, ciprofloxacin, methotrexate, methylprednisolone, gentamicin, tobramycin, magnesium sulfate (when concentrated), bicarbonate. Many others: NO RELIABLE DATA — treat as incompatible. Use a dedicated propofol line where possible; if shared, restrict to confirmed compatible agents and use micro-bore proximal injection ports. Use of in-line filter on a propofol line is NOT recommended (filter pore < 5 µm captures lipid).
alternative: Dedicated propofol line. If lines limited and drug not on confirmed-compatible list: temporarily pause propofol, flush with NS, give bolus drug, flush NS, resume.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Compatibility of propofol injectable emulsion with selected drugs during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.
ASHP King Guide — propofol.

oneLiner: Norepinephrine is inactivated in alkaline solution — colour darkens (oxidation), potency lost. Do NOT mix with bicarbonate; do not co-infuse via the same lumen without flush.
notes: Catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, isoprenaline) are oxidised by alkaline solutions, producing visible pink/brown discolouration and rapid loss of pressor activity. ALWAYS use a separate lumen for bicarbonate boluses; if only one lumen available, pause pressor, flush thoroughly with NS, push bicarb, flush again, restart pressor. The same warning applies to aminophylline, furosemide and any other strongly alkaline drugs co-administered with catecholamines.
alternative: Use a dedicated lumen for vasopressors. For acute bicarbonate boluses on a single-lumen line: pause-flush-bicarb-flush-resume.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Norepinephrine.
King Guide to Parenteral Admixtures — catecholamine alkaline incompatibility.

oneLiner: Epinephrine oxidises in alkaline solution (visible browning, loss of potency). Same separation rule as norepinephrine.
notes: Same mechanism as norepinephrine: catecholamine oxidation in alkaline medium. Separate lumen for bicarb; if not possible, pause-flush-bicarb-flush-resume. This is particularly relevant in cardiac arrest where epinephrine and sodium bicarbonate are commonly given through the same peripheral line under time pressure — flush thoroughly between them.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Epinephrine.

oneLiner: Forms insoluble calcium carbonate — visible white precipitate, line occlusion. Separate lumen or pause-flush-bicarb-flush-resume.
notes: Ca²⁺ + 2 HCO₃⁻ → CaCO₃ + H₂CO₃ (insoluble precipitate). Common emergency-room mistake: pushing calcium gluconate and bicarbonate through the same peripheral line during hyperkalaemia or cardiac arrest — line blocks within seconds with a white precipitate. Always use separate lumens or flush thoroughly between pushes. Particularly relevant in massive transfusion (Ca + citrated blood) and in neonatal resuscitation.
alternative: Separate lumen; if single line, push Ca, flush 20 mL NS, push bicarb, flush 20 mL NS.

references.label: ASHP King Guide — Calcium / Sodium bicarbonate.

oneLiner: Visible precipitate at Y-site. Do not co-infuse on the same line concurrently; separate lines or stagger doses with flush.
notes: Trissel-confirmed Y-site incompatible — visible precipitate within minutes when mixed at clinical concentrations. The combination is one of the most common empiric ICU regimens (vancomycin + pip-tazo for hospital-acquired pneumonia / sepsis) so the incompatibility is frequently relevant. Note that this is separate from the well-publicised vancomycin-pip-tazo AKI signal (which is a clinical interaction, not a chemical compatibility issue).
alternative: Use separate IV lines, or stagger administration on the same line with a thorough NS flush between doses.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vancomycin.
King Guide to Parenteral Admixtures — vancomycin compatibility tables.

oneLiner: Vancomycin + heparin → visible precipitate at Y-site. Use separate lumens, or flush thoroughly between.
notes: Documented incompatibility (precipitate, loss of potency for both drugs). Relevant when both run on the same central line (e.g. vancomycin for line sepsis + therapeutic heparin in the same critical-care patient). For heparin-locked central lines, flush thoroughly with NS before and after vancomycin doses.
alternative: Separate lumen on a multi-lumen central line. If only one lumen: flush 10 mL NS before and after vancomycin push / infusion.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vancomycin.

drugB: Common Y-site partners (epinephrine, vasopressin, dobutamine, dexmedetomidine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, insulin, KCl)
oneLiner: Norepinephrine is Y-site compatible with most other vasoactive infusions and ICU staples at typical concentrations — the main exceptions are alkaline drugs (bicarb, aminophylline, furosemide).
notes: Trissel / King Guide confirmed compatible at typical ICU concentrations (norepinephrine 16-128 µg/mL, partners at standard infusion concentrations): epinephrine, vasopressin (note: vasopressin should ideally run on its own line for steady-state dosing but is Y-site compatible if needed), dobutamine, dexmedetomidine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol (one of the few — confirmed), insulin (regular human), KCl (20-40 mmol/L), magnesium sulfate, heparin, hydrocortisone, ondansetron, pantoprazole, lorazepam. Discoloration may occur with prolonged contact — observe.
alternative: If discolouration appears, separate the lines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Norepinephrine Y-site.
ASHP King Guide — vasoactive infusion compatibility.

drugB: Common Y-site partners (norepinephrine, epinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, insulin)
oneLiner: Vasopressin is generally Y-site compatible with the common ICU vasoactive and sedative infusions, but is adsorbed by PVC (use polyolefin / non-DEHP sets where available) and best run on its own line for steady-state dosing.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, regular insulin, heparin. Adsorbs to PVC (~ 10-20% loss over typical infusion length) — non-PVC tubing preferred for reliable dosing. For accurate titration, give via its own line where feasible.
alternative: Non-PVC tubing; dedicated line for titration accuracy.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin.

oneLiner: Compatible — commonly co-infused as ICU sedation/analgesia. No reported chemical incompatibility at clinical concentrations.
notes: Both stable in NS and D5W. Y-site compatible and syringe-compatible at typical infusion concentrations (fentanyl 10-50 µg/mL, midazolam 1-5 mg/mL). Pharmacodynamic synergy on respiratory depression is the clinical concern, not chemical incompatibility — titrate both with that in mind.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Fentanyl / Midazolam.

drugB: Most acidic drugs (catecholamines, midazolam, ondansetron, amiodarone, ciprofloxacin, vancomycin, dobutamine)
oneLiner: Furosemide is highly alkaline (pH 8.5-9) — visible precipitate with most acidic drugs at Y-site. Separate line or flush thoroughly.
notes: Furosemide is unstable below pH 5.5 — it crystallises out. Documented incompatible at Y-site with most catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dobutamine, dopamine), midazolam (acidic), ondansetron, amiodarone, ciprofloxacin, vancomycin, metoclopramide, labetalol. Use a dedicated lumen for furosemide infusions, or flush thoroughly (20 mL NS) before and after a furosemide push. Bumetanide has the same alkalinity profile.
alternative: Dedicated lumen for continuous furosemide. For intermittent boluses on a shared line: 20 mL NS flush before + after.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Furosemide.

drugB: Peripheral IV access (compatibility with the line, not a partner drug)
oneLiner: Concentrated KCl is a high-alert medication — peripheral infusion max 40 mmol/L at ≤ 10 mmol/h to avoid phlebitis; > 40 mmol/L MUST be central. Never IV push neat KCl.
notes: Although technically a route question rather than a drug-pair compatibility, KCl administration is one of the most common patient-safety incidents and warrants a dedicated reference. Peripheral: ≤ 40 mmol/L concentration, ≤ 10 mmol/h infusion rate (phlebitis ceiling). Central: up to 100 mmol/L, ≤ 20 mmol/h (continuous cardiac monitoring needed). Bolus IV push of neat KCl is rapidly fatal (cardiac arrest) — never administer as a push. Always dilute and label as a high-alert drug; double-check the patient and the bag with a second clinician.
alternative: For mild hypokalaemia: oral KCl (Slow K, Sando-K) is preferred — equally effective, no infusion risk.

references.label: ISMP High-Alert Medications list.
WHO List of High Alert Medications.

oneLiner: Forms insoluble precipitate (magnesium-calcium salts). Never mix in the same bag or syringe; separate lines or pause-flush sequence on a single line.
notes: Common scenario: a patient on magnesium sulfate infusion for pre-eclampsia who develops symptomatic magnesium toxicity (loss of patellar reflexes, respiratory depression). The treatment is calcium gluconate IV — but cannot be given through the same line / lumen as the magnesium. Stop magnesium infusion, FLUSH line, then push calcium via the same line (or use a separate access).
alternative: Stop Mg infusion → flush line with NS → push Ca → resume only after toxicity resolves.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Magnesium sulfate.
WHO recommendations on prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

drugA: Total parenteral nutrition (TPN — amino acid + dextrose + lipid)
oneLiner: TPN is a complex emulsion — destabilises with most co-administered drugs (lipid coalescence, precipitation, line occlusion). Run TPN through its OWN dedicated lumen.
notes: TPN should be administered through its OWN dedicated central line lumen. Very few drugs have been formally studied for Y-site compatibility with 3-in-1 TPN admixtures: documented compatible (at Y-site only): insulin (regular), ranitidine, famotidine, octreotide, low-dose dopamine. INCOMPATIBLE or no-data — treat as incompatible: all antibiotics, vasopressors, electrolytes (additives are mixed into the TPN bag by pharmacy ONLY), phenytoin, midazolam, morphine, heparin (some 2-in-1 amino acid + dextrose are heparin-compatible — verify locally). Particular danger: calcium + phosphate solubility curve — these must be balanced when the bag is compounded; never add Ca or PO₄ at the bedside.
alternative: Dedicated TPN lumen on a multi-lumen central line. Co-administer other drugs through a different lumen.

references.label: ASPEN parenteral nutrition safety consensus recommendations. JPEN 2014.
ASHP King Guide — TPN compatibility.

drugB: PVC infusion sets and bags (line/container compatibility — not a drug pair)
oneLiner: Regular insulin adsorbs to PVC and glass (up to ~ 30% loss) — flush 20-50 mL of the diluted insulin infusion through the line BEFORE connecting to the patient, to saturate the binding sites.
notes: When preparing a continuous insulin infusion (e.g. 50 units in 50 mL NS for DKA), the first ~ 20-50 mL run through the line will be subtherapeutic due to adsorption onto the PVC tubing and bag — this is why DKA infusion protocols specify 'prime the line with 20-50 mL of the prepared infusion and discard before connecting to the patient'. Non-PVC tubing (polyolefin, polyurethane) has much less adsorption. Y-site compatibility with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol — all confirmed compatible (insulin is commonly co-infused on a single lumen with ICU drips).
alternative: Use non-PVC tubing where available. If PVC: prime + discard 20-50 mL before patient connection.

references.label: ASHP King Guide — Insulin admixture stability.
JBDS-IP guideline: Management of DKA in adults.

oneLiner: Metronidazole is Y-site compatible with most common antibiotics (ceftriaxone, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, vancomycin, gentamicin) and many ICU drugs — one of the more permissive co-administration agents.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with most beta-lactams (ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, imipenem, aztreonam), vancomycin (yes — confirmed Y-site compatible despite the vancomycin + pip-tazo separate-line rule), aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, fluconazole, fentanyl, morphine, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, heparin. Few documented incompatibilities — useful for co-infusion when line access is limited.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Metronidazole.

drugB: Common ICU partners (vasopressors, sedation, vancomycin, metronidazole)
oneLiner: Meropenem is Y-site compatible with most common ICU drugs at clinical concentrations. Avoid co-infusion with valproate (well-known interaction reduces valproate levels — clinical, not chemical).
notes: Y-site compatible with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, vancomycin, metronidazole, heparin. Stability in solution is the bigger practical concern: meropenem is stable in NS for ~ 4 h at room temperature, ~ 24 h refrigerated; D5W reduces stability significantly (degradation > 10% within 1 h). Use NS, not D5W. Extended infusion (3-4 h) is supported by NS stability data but requires a fresh bag every 3-4 h. Valproate: not a chemical compatibility issue but a clinical drug interaction — meropenem (and other carbapenems) dramatically reduce valproate plasma levels, risking seizure breakthrough.
alternative: For valproate-treated patients: avoid carbapenems if possible; use alternative anti-pseudomonal (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Meropenem.
Park MK et al. Meropenem-valproate interaction. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2012.

oneLiner: Ciprofloxacin has poor compatibility — precipitates with most heparin-containing solutions, aminophylline, furosemide, dexamethasone, magnesium and many beta-lactams. Y-site with caution.
notes: Documented incompatible at Y-site: heparin (visible precipitate), aminophylline, furosemide, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone, magnesium sulfate, ampicillin, cefepime, cefoperazone, ceftriaxone (visible cloudiness — flush thoroughly between), propofol, meropenem (some studies), erythromycin. Compatible at Y-site: vancomycin (in some studies — verify locally), morphine, midazolam, ondansetron, tobramycin (if administered through pump, not as Y-site bolus). Dilute to ≤ 2 mg/mL; infuse over 60 min minimum to reduce phlebitis. Note: divalent cation co-administration (Mg, Ca, Al, Zn) clinically reduces ciprofloxacin absorption (with oral) but is also a chemical issue at IV Y-site with high-concentration cation infusions.
alternative: Dedicated line for ciprofloxacin infusion. If single-line: flush thoroughly between drugs.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ciprofloxacin.

oneLiner: Ondansetron is Y-site compatible with most ICU + chemo agents at typical concentrations. Notable exceptions: alkaline solutions (5-FU, sodium bicarbonate, furosemide, aciclovir, ampicillin, ceftriaxone occasionally).
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone, midazolam, propofol, lorazepam, dexmedetomidine, vancomycin, metronidazole, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate (low concentration). Incompatible at Y-site with sodium bicarbonate, furosemide, 5-FU, ampicillin (variable), aciclovir, methylprednisolone (some preparations), pantoprazole (acidic incompatibility).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ondansetron.

oneLiner: Pantoprazole is very pH-sensitive (stable at pH ≥ 9; precipitates rapidly at neutral / acidic pH). Use NS or D5W, flush thoroughly before and after, do not co-infuse with most other drugs.
notes: Documented Y-site incompatible with most things: catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine — well-documented precipitate), midazolam, fentanyl, morphine, KCl, calcium, magnesium, vancomycin, ondansetron, metoclopramide, ciprofloxacin. Compatible (Y-site, limited list): heparin, ranitidine, octreotide. Best practice: pantoprazole infusion on a dedicated lumen. If single-line: flush 10-20 mL NS before and after each pantoprazole administration.
alternative: Dedicated lumen, or substitute with omeprazole infusion (similar compatibility issues but better in NS).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Pantoprazole.

oneLiner: Heparin is broadly compatible with sedation, analgesia, and most pressors, but INCOMPATIBLE with several common antibiotics (vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, tobramycin at higher concentrations).
notes: Y-site COMPATIBLE with: fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, vasopressin, insulin (regular), pantoprazole, ranitidine, ondansetron, metronidazole, metoclopramide, KCl, magnesium sulfate. INCOMPATIBLE: vancomycin (precipitate), ciprofloxacin (precipitate), gentamicin (loss of potency at high heparin concentrations — clinical relevance is debated), tobramycin (similar), amiodarone (precipitate), aminoglycosides generally (consider separate line), diazepam (precipitate). Heparin is often run as a continuous infusion on a single ICU line shared with sedation and vasopressors — that combination is well-tolerated; the antibiotic dose pushes need to go through a different lumen or via a thorough flush.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Heparin.

oneLiner: Dexmedetomidine is Y-site compatible with the standard ICU vasoactive + sedation + analgesia infusions. No major documented incompatibilities.
notes: Compatible at Y-site (Trissel-confirmed at typical clinical concentrations): fentanyl, alfentanil, remifentanil, morphine, hydromorphone, midazolam, lorazepam, propofol, ketamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin, dopamine, dobutamine, insulin, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, vancomycin, metronidazole, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, hydrocortisone, methylprednisolone, ondansetron, esmolol, labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerin. Stable in NS and D5W. Adsorbs minimally to PVC.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dexmedetomidine.
Wagner DS et al. Compatibility of dexmedetomidine with selected medications during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2009.

oneLiner: Tranexamic acid is INCOMPATIBLE with blood products in the same line (acts as a procoagulant locally) and with thrombolytics (mechanistic antagonism). Use a separate line.
notes: Do not mix tranexamic acid in the same bag or line as packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma, platelets, or cryoprecipitate — the antifibrinolytic activity in the line can promote local clot formation in transfused product. Mechanistically antagonistic to thrombolytics (alteplase, tenecteplase) — do not co-administer; tranexamic acid is sometimes given AFTER lysis-related bleed but on a separate line, well after the lytic infusion has stopped. Compatible with most NS / D5W infusion partners (vasopressors, sedation, analgesia).
alternative: Separate line for tranexamic acid when transfusing.

references.label: TXA injection — manufacturer SmPC.
CRASH-2 administration protocol.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical ICU concentrations. Both catecholamines tolerate co-infusion via the same lumen.
notes: Both stable in NS or D5W. Y-site compatible at standard pressor concentrations. Avoid alkaline co-infusates (bicarbonate, aminophylline, furosemide) on the same lumen — catecholamine oxidation will affect both. Titrate each independently and label clearly to avoid bolus errors when one drip is being adjusted.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Norepinephrine / Epinephrine Y-site.
ASHP King Guide — catecholamine co-administration.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — the standard septic-shock pressor pairing. Vasopressin's PVC adsorption is the only practical issue.
notes: Compatible at clinical concentrations during simulated Y-site administration. Vasopressin adsorbs to PVC tubing — non-PVC sets preferred for titration accuracy. Often co-infused on a single central-line lumen as the standard septic-shock regimen.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at standard ICU concentrations — the canonical 'inopressor' combination for septic cardiomyopathy.
notes: Both catecholamines, compatible in NS or D5W during Y-site administration. Avoid alkaline co-infusates on the shared lumen. Pink/brown discolouration over time on the shared line indicates oxidation — change set and check pressor activity.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dobutamine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible. Same alkaline-incompatibility caveats as for any catecholamine pair.
notes: Compatible at typical infusion concentrations. Avoid co-administration on the same lumen with bicarbonate, aminophylline or furosemide — alkalinity will oxidise both catecholamines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dopamine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at clinical pressor concentrations.
notes: Both are catechol-like alpha agonists. Co-administration tolerated at typical concentrations in NS or D5W. Alkaline-drug caveats apply. Commonly seen in anaesthesia hand-over where phenylephrine boluses are tapered as norepinephrine is started.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Phenylephrine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at standard ICU concentrations.
notes: Tolerated at clinical concentrations. PVC adsorption applies to vasopressin. Avoid alkaline co-infusates.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin / Epinephrine.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical ICU concentrations.
notes: Both catecholamines; compatible in NS or D5W during simulated Y-site administration. Same alkalinity warnings — avoid bicarbonate / furosemide on the shared lumen.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dobutamine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Tolerated at clinical concentrations. Both prone to oxidation in alkaline media — keep bicarbonate off the shared lumen.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dopamine / Epinephrine.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Compatible at clinical concentrations during simulated Y-site administration. Vasopressin PVC-adsorption caveat applies — use non-PVC tubing where possible.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical clinical concentrations.
notes: Compatible during simulated Y-site administration. PVC-adsorption caveat for vasopressin.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Tolerated at clinical concentrations. PVC-adsorption caveat for vasopressin.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Phenylephrine / Vasopressin.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Both catecholamines; tolerate co-infusion in NS or D5W. Avoid alkaline co-infusates on the shared lumen.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dobutamine / Dopamine.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at clinical concentrations.
notes: Tolerated during simulated Y-site administration. Both vasoactive catechol-like agents in mild-to-moderate ICU concentrations.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Tolerated at clinical pressor concentrations.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Compatible during simulated Y-site administration. Same alkalinity caveats as for any catecholamine.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — one of the small list of confirmed-stable partners for the propofol lipid emulsion.
notes: Confirmed Y-site compatible at typical sedation concentrations (propofol 10 mg/mL, fentanyl 10-50 µg/mL). Combination is the classic ICU mechanical-ventilation regimen. Pharmacodynamic synergy on hypotension and respiratory drive is the clinical issue, not chemical compatibility.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Compatibility of propofol injectable emulsion with selected drugs during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical sedation concentrations.
notes: Trissel-confirmed Y-site compatible. The lipid emulsion of propofol tolerates midazolam at clinical concentrations. Confirm visually for any oiling on a shared lumen.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Compatibility of propofol injectable emulsion with selected drugs during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at clinical sedation concentrations.
notes: Confirmed Y-site compatible during simulated co-administration. Commonly co-titrated during ventilator weaning where dexmedetomidine replaces deep sedation.

references.label: Wagner DS et al. Compatibility of dexmedetomidine with selected medications during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2009.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — used as 'ketofol' for procedural sedation.
notes: Confirmed Y-site compatible. Often pre-mixed in the same syringe ('ketofol') for procedural sedation in the ED at varying ratios (1:1 to 4:1 propofol:ketamine). Verify the local protocol's mixing ratio and observe the syringe for any oiling before injection.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Propofol Y-site compatibility.
Andolfatto G et al. Ketamine-propofol combination (ketofol) for procedural sedation. Ann Emerg Med 2012.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — the standard TIVA pairing.

CaCl₂ is more bioavailable and faster-acting (preferred in arrest, hyperkalaemia, citrate intoxication during massive transfusion) but markedly more irritant — extravasation causes severe necrosis. Documented incompatible: amphotericin B, ceftriaxone, diazepam, erythromycin, phenytoin. Manufacturer instructs flushing the line before and after.

references.label: Linezolid (Zyvox) — manufacturer prescribing information.
Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Linezolid.

oneLiner: Aciclovir is alkaline (pH ~ 11) — precipitates with many acidic drugs at Y-site.
notes: Y-site incompatible with most catecholamines, ondansetron, dobutamine, dopamine, fentanyl (variable), midazolam, morphine (variable), aminoglycosides, vancomycin (precipitate). Compatible with metronidazole, ceftriaxone, heparin, KCl. Best practice: dedicated line; if shared, flush thoroughly before and after.
alternative: Dedicated line; NS flush between staggered doses.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Acyclovir.

oneLiner: Hydrocortisone is Y-site compatible with most common ICU drugs.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, vasopressin, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, vancomycin, metronidazole, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, insulin. Documented Y-site incompatible: ciprofloxacin, diazepam, phenytoin, midazolam (some studies — variable).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Hydrocortisone Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site incompatible — destabilises propofol lipid emulsion.
notes: Trissel-listed propofol Y-site incompatibility. Use separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical clinical concentrations.
notes: Tolerated during simulated Y-site administration. Common ICU combination for analgo-sedation with concurrent vasopressor support.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ketamine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with the standard ICU pressors (norepinephrine, epinephrine, vasopressin).
notes: Tolerated at clinical concentrations. Useful in vasoplegic patients where ketamine's sympathomimetic effect is desired.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ketamine.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Tolerated during simulated Y-site administration. Combination occurs in haemorrhagic stroke patients where BP control needs both up-titration and rapid down-titration capability.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Nicardipine Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. Adsorbs to PVC — use non-PVC tubing for accurate dosing.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, vancomycin, metronidazole, ondansetron. Adsorbs significantly onto PVC tubing — use non-PVC (polyethylene, polyolefin) sets to deliver the labelled dose.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Nitroglycerin Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs at typical concentrations.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, vancomycin, metronidazole. Documented incompatible: furosemide, sodium bicarbonate, diazepam, thiopental.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Esmolol Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs at typical concentrations. Incompatible with furosemide, bicarbonate.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol (variable — verify locally), dexmedetomidine, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate. Documented incompatible: furosemide, sodium bicarbonate, nafcillin, thiopental.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Labetalol Y-site.

drugB: Packed red cells / FFP / platelets / cryoprecipitate
oneLiner: Do not mix in the same line or bag — local antifibrinolytic activity risks clot formation in transfused product.
notes: Tranexamic acid blocks plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis; in the line, this can promote clot formation in transfused product before delivery to the patient. Use a separate line for TXA when transfusing.
alternative: Separate line for TXA during transfusion.

references.label: Tranexamic acid injection — manufacturer SmPC.

oneLiner: Do not co-administer through the same line — calcium reverses the citrate anticoagulation and forms a clot in the line.
notes: Citrate in stored blood chelates calcium to prevent clotting in the bag; adding calcium back upstream reverses this and produces a clot in the line. In massive transfusion where calcium replacement is needed (citrate-induced hypocalcaemia), give calcium via a separate access — never the transfusion line.
alternative: Separate line for calcium replacement during massive transfusion.

references.label: AABB Technical Manual — massive transfusion.

oneLiner: Calcium in Ringer's reverses citrate anticoagulation — clot in the line. Use NS as the running fluid for transfusion.
notes: Long-standing transfusion teaching: do not run packed red cells in the same line as Ringer's lactate or any calcium-containing fluid — the calcium reverses citrate anticoagulation. Practical evidence on the absolute size of the risk is mixed for modern leukoreduced product, but the standard remains NS as the transfusion fluid.
alternative: Use NS as the running fluid for transfusions.

references.label: AABB Technical Manual — administration of blood components.

drugA: IV lipid emulsion (20% Intralipid as LAST antidote, or as TPN component)
drugB: Most other IV drugs at Y-site
oneLiner: Lipid emulsion is destabilised by most drugs — when given as LAST antidote, use a dedicated line.
notes: 20% lipid emulsion (Intralipid) is the antidote for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) and is also a TPN component. Same compatibility limitations as propofol's lipid vehicle — most drugs destabilise the emulsion (lipid coalescence, droplet enlargement). When administering as LAST antidote, use a dedicated line; the patient is usually already in arrest with multiple other lines available.
alternative: Dedicated line for lipid bolus / infusion.

references.label: ASRA Practice Advisory on Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. 2018.

oneLiner: Insulin may be compounded into the TPN bag by pharmacy — routine practice for hyperglycaemia on TPN.
notes: Pharmacy-compounded insulin in the TPN bag (typically 0.05-0.15 unit per gram of dextrose, individualised) is routine. Adsorption to PVC reduces delivered dose vs labelled; the local TPN service adjusts. Do not add insulin to the bag at the bedside.

references.label: ASPEN parenteral nutrition safety consensus recommendations. JPEN 2014.

oneLiner: Octreotide is Y-site compatible with TPN at typical infusion concentrations.
notes: Tolerated at typical clinical concentrations during simulated Y-site administration. Useful for chylothorax / high-output fistula patients on TPN.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Octreotide / TPN.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with TPN at typical infusion concentrations.
notes: Tolerated during simulated Y-site administration; some institutions compound famotidine / ranitidine into the TPN bag.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — TPN / H2 blockers.

drugB: Most IV drugs and PVC tubing
oneLiner: Diazepam is highly lipophilic and adsorbs heavily to PVC; precipitates on dilution and with most co-infusates. Use a dedicated route, push slowly into a large vein.
notes: Diazepam in propylene-glycol vehicle precipitates on contact with most aqueous solutions and adsorbs significantly to PVC tubing. Do not mix in infusion bags. Push slowly (≤ 5 mg/min) directly into a large vein, ideally close to the IV catheter. Lorazepam or midazolam are preferred where IV access is the limiting factor.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Diazepam.

oneLiner: Clinical (not chemical) interaction: carbapenems dramatically reduce valproate plasma levels — seizure breakthrough risk.
notes: Mechanism is enhanced glucuronidation and intracellular distribution of valproate triggered by carbapenems. Levels can drop > 50 % within 24 h. Avoid the combination in valproate-treated epilepsy patients; if a carbapenem is essential, switch the anticonvulsant or use levetiracetam cover.
alternative: Use cefepime or pip-tazo if anti-pseudomonal cover is needed; or load with an alternative anticonvulsant.

references.label: Park MK et al. Meropenem-valproate interaction. Am J Health Syst Pharm 2012.
BNF / meropenem-valproate interaction.

oneLiner: Y-site data with most drugs is limited — manufacturer recommends not mixing with other infusions in the same container.
notes: Albumin is a complex protein solution; mixing risks denaturation. Manufacturer SmPC instructs that albumin should not be mixed with other medicinal products. At Y-site, very few formal compatibility studies; default to a separate line.

references.label: Human albumin solution — manufacturer SmPC.

oneLiner: Mannitol crystallises in solution if cooled — warm to dissolve before use, and use an in-line filter. Limited Y-site data; default to a separate line.
notes: 20 % mannitol may crystallise on storage or cooling — inspect each bag and warm to redissolve crystals before infusion. Use an in-line filter (0.22 µm) to catch any residual crystal. Limited Y-site data with most drugs; use a separate line for osmotherapy.

references.label: Mannitol — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at clinical concentrations.
notes: Tolerated at typical infusion concentrations during simulated Y-site administration.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Remifentanil Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — listed among Trissel-confirmed propofol partners.
notes: Confirmed Y-site compatible at clinical concentrations during simulated administration.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible.
notes: Listed among Trissel-confirmed propofol partners. Standard TIVA component.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible — listed among Trissel-confirmed propofol partners.
notes: Confirmed Y-site compatible at clinical concentrations during simulated administration. Clinically uncommon scenario, but documented compatible.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Visible precipitate at Y-site (acidic ciprofloxacin + alkaline aminophylline).
notes: Documented Y-site incompatibility. Use separate lines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ciprofloxacin.

oneLiner: Destabilises propofol emulsion at Y-site — use separate lumens.
notes: Trissel-listed propofol Y-site incompatibility (acidic ciprofloxacin destabilises the lipid emulsion).

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.

oneLiner: Visible precipitate at Y-site.
notes: Documented Y-site precipitate at typical clinical concentrations. Separate lines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ciprofloxacin.

oneLiner: Never draw a penicillin + aminoglycoside in the same syringe — chemical inactivation of the aminoglycoside.
notes: Penicillins inactivate aminoglycosides on prolonged contact in solution; the inactivation accelerates at the high concentrations found in syringes pre-administration. Never combine in a single syringe — draw and administer separately.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ampicillin / Gentamicin.

oneLiner: Neonates often have a single UVC / peripheral cannula carrying TPN + lipid + multiple drugs — verify each pair before adding, never extrapolate adult data without checking pharmacy.
notes: Neonatal IV management compresses many simultaneous infusions onto very limited access. Recurring high-mortality patterns: ceftriaxone + Ca (absolute contraindication < 28 days), ampicillin + gentamicin syringe co-mix (inactivation), insulin adsorption on micro-bore PVC. The local NICU pharmacy maintains a compatibility chart — defer to it rather than to adult Trissel summaries.
alternative: Defer to local NICU compatibility chart for each pair.

references.label: Neonatal Formulary / BNFc — IV compatibility.

oneLiner: Octreotide is Y-site compatible with most common ICU drugs and TPN.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron, vancomycin, metronidazole, TPN.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Octreotide.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. Notable incompatibilities: furosemide, sodium bicarbonate, pantoprazole.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol (variable), heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron, vancomycin, metronidazole. Incompatible: furosemide, sodium bicarbonate, pantoprazole, cisplatin, ampicillin (variable).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Metoclopramide.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. Incompatible at Y-site with ciprofloxacin, diphenhydramine (some studies), midazolam (variable).
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, propofol, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron, vancomycin, metronidazole. Incompatible: ciprofloxacin, glycopyrrolate, midazolam (variable — verify locally).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dexamethasone Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, ondansetron, vancomycin, heparin, KCl. Documented incompatibilities are sparse but include some cephalosporins and dexamethasone (variable).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Diphenhydramine.

oneLiner: Clindamycin is Y-site compatible with most common ICU drugs.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, vancomycin (some studies), metronidazole, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron. Documented Y-site incompatible: aminophylline, ceftriaxone (some studies), phenytoin.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Clindamycin Y-site.

oneLiner: Aztreonam is Y-site compatible with most common ICU drugs and many other antibiotics.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, vancomycin, metronidazole, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron. Same aminoglycoside-inactivation rule applies in solution (separate lines).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Aztreonam Y-site.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. Stability in solution limits hang time — use NS, reconstitute fresh.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, vancomycin, metronidazole, heparin, KCl. Like meropenem, stability in solution is the limiting factor — use NS, change bag every 4 h. Aminoglycoside inactivation in solution rule applies.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Imipenem-cilastatin.

oneLiner: Cefepime is Y-site compatible with most ICU sedation / pressor lines; incompatible with vancomycin, aminoglycosides, metronidazole (some studies).
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron. Documented incompatible: vancomycin, aminoglycosides (separate lines), metronidazole (variable — verify locally).

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Cefepime Y-site.

oneLiner: Ceftazidime is Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. Aminoglycoside-inactivation rule applies.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, vancomycin (most studies), heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron, metronidazole. Aminoglycosides: separate lines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Ceftazidime Y-site.

oneLiner: Phenytoin must be diluted in NS only and infused within 1 h of preparation; precipitates in dextrose or on prolonged standing.
notes: Diluent: 0.9% NaCl only. Final concentration ≤ 10 mg/mL. Infuse within 1 h of dilution. Visually inspect for any precipitate before and during infusion — discard if cloudy. Use an in-line 0.22-0.45 µm filter. Maximum rate ≤ 50 mg/min adult.
alternative: Fosphenytoin (compatible with any standard fluid; no filter required).

references.label: Phenytoin sodium injection SmPC.

oneLiner: Fosphenytoin (water-soluble phenytoin pro-drug) is compatible with both NS and D5W, requires no in-line filter, and can be loaded faster than phenytoin.
notes: Loading rate up to 150 mg PE/min adult (3 mg PE/kg/min paediatric). NS or D5W diluent. Y-site compatibility profile broadly favourable. Preferred over phenytoin where available, particularly in patients with difficult IV access or who need other drugs on the same line.

references.label: ASHP Therapeutic Position Statement on the use of fosphenytoin.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible with most ICU drugs. No major documented incompatibilities at clinical concentrations.
notes: Compatible at Y-site with norepinephrine, fentanyl, midazolam, propofol, dexmedetomidine, vancomycin, metronidazole, heparin, KCl, magnesium sulfate, ondansetron. Stable in NS or D5W.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Levetiracetam Y-site.

oneLiner: Limited Y-site data — treat as conditional, separate lumens where possible.
notes: Trissel does not list a definitive Y-site study. Practical advice: keep bicarbonate on a separate lumen from the insulin infusion in DKA where bicarbonate is occasionally used.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Insulin (limited bicarbonate data).

drugA: Diluent choice: NS vs D5W vs Ringer's
oneLiner: Always check the drug-specific diluent — wrong fluid degrades some drugs rapidly. Key examples: amiodarone D5W only, phenytoin NS only, ceftriaxone never in Ca-containing fluid.
notes: Heuristic — but always verify the SmPC: amiodarone D5W only (precipitates in NS); phenytoin NS only (precipitates in D5W); ceftriaxone NS or D5W, never Ringer's / Hartmann's; pantoprazole NS or D5W; ampicillin NS only (poor D5W stability); most aminoglycosides NS or D5W; most beta-lactams NS or D5W. Lipid emulsions (propofol, Intralipid) destabilise in many diluents — give undiluted via dedicated lumen.

references.label: BNF / SmPC of each individual drug — diluent compatibility section.

oneLiner: Ampicillin has poor stability in dextrose — degrades within hours. Use NS, prepare fresh, infuse promptly.
notes: Ampicillin in NS is stable at room temperature for several hours; in D5W stability is much shorter (degradation > 10 % within a few hours). Use NS as diluent and infuse promptly after reconstitution.
alternative: Use NS; infuse within 1 h of reconstitution.

references.label: Ampicillin sodium injection — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Phosphate + calcium precipitates as Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Do not co-administer; pharmacy-compound only for TPN.
notes: Standard precipitation issue. Phosphate-containing IV replacement must use a different lumen from calcium replacement, separated in time.

references.label: ASPEN — calcium/phosphate solubility in PN.

oneLiner: Risk of magnesium carbonate / hydroxide precipitate in concentrated mixtures.
notes: Concentrated magnesium and bicarbonate together can precipitate as Mg(OH)₂ / MgCO₃. Use separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Magnesium sulfate / Sodium bicarbonate.

drugB: Maintenance bag preparation — pre-mixed bags preferred
oneLiner: Pre-mixed bags (e.g. 20 / 40 mmol KCl in NS or D5W) are preferred over bedside addition — bedside mixing is a known cause of fatal layering errors.
notes: When KCl is added to a hanging bag at the bedside and not adequately mixed, concentrated KCl layers at the bottom (denser than NS / D5W); the first portion infused delivers a near-bolus and has caused cardiac arrests. ISMP and WHO recommend pharmacy-prepared pre-mixed bags. If bedside addition is unavoidable, invert the bag at least 10 times to ensure complete mixing before hanging.

references.label: ISMP High-Alert Medications list — concentrated potassium chloride.
WHO List of High Alert Medications.

oneLiner: Lipid-containing 3-in-1 TPN destabilises with most co-infusates — use a dedicated lumen.
notes: Same compatibility issues as propofol's lipid vehicle but compounded by the dextrose + amino acid + electrolytes already in the bag. Use a dedicated lumen; the few Y-site compatible additions (insulin, octreotide, ranitidine, famotidine) are the only exceptions.

references.label: ASPEN parenteral nutrition safety consensus recommendations.

oneLiner: Vasopressin adsorbs to PVC tubing (~ 10-20 % loss). Use non-PVC tubing for titration accuracy in septic shock.
notes: Tubing-related delivery loss matters most when small fixed doses are titrated; for the typical 0.03 unit/min infusion in septic shock, a 10-20 % loss can be clinically meaningful. Polyolefin or polyurethane sets reduce the loss substantially.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin (PVC adsorption).

oneLiner: Amiodarone in PVC tubing leaches DEHP plasticiser; use non-PVC (polyolefin) sets for prolonged infusion.
notes: Amiodarone is a powerful solvent for the DEHP plasticiser in PVC tubing. For short emergency infusions (loading dose) PVC is acceptable, but prolonged maintenance infusions should use non-DEHP / polyolefin tubing where available, both to limit DEHP exposure and to maintain dose accuracy.

references.label: Cordarone IV (amiodarone HCl) — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Nitroglycerin adsorbs significantly to PVC (~ 40-80% loss in standard sets). Use non-PVC tubing.
notes: Standard PVC tubing absorbs a large fraction of the infused nitroglycerin (40-80% depending on rate and length of tubing). Non-PVC tubing (polyethylene-lined, polyolefin) is required to deliver the labelled dose. This is a longstanding manufacturer warning.

references.label: Nitroglycerin injection — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Tacrolimus IV adsorbs to PVC and leaches phthalates — use non-PVC tubing and glass containers.
notes: Manufacturer requires dilution in glass or non-PVC bag and administration via non-PVC tubing due to phthalate leaching and adsorption. Standard PVC reduces delivered dose.

references.label: Tacrolimus IV — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Limited Y-site data — separate lumens preferred.
notes: Trissel does not list a definitive Y-site study. Separate lumen for bicarbonate boluses; pause-flush sequence on a single line.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Sodium bicarbonate (limited data).

oneLiner: Morphine precipitates in alkaline solution (free-base separation).
notes: Acidic morphine salt precipitates as free base in alkaline media. Use separate lumens; pause-flush sequence on single-line access.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Morphine.

oneLiner: Acidic vancomycin precipitates with alkaline bicarbonate at Y-site.
notes: Visible precipitate at typical clinical concentrations. Use separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vancomycin / Sodium bicarbonate.

oneLiner: Y-site compatible at typical infusion concentrations — but never mix in the same bag or syringe.
notes: Trissel-listed compatible at typical clinical concentrations during simulated Y-site administration. Mixing in the same bag is NOT recommended (binding / inactivation on prolonged contact). Useful when only two lumens available and pip-tazo cannot be used.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vancomycin Y-site.

oneLiner: Heparin lock fluid + vancomycin can precipitate — flush thoroughly with NS before and after vancomycin administration.
notes: Even small residual heparin lock concentrations in the line can produce a visible precipitate with vancomycin. Flush the lumen with at least 10 mL NS before starting and after finishing the vancomycin infusion.
alternative: NS flush before and after vancomycin on heparin-locked lines.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vancomycin / Heparin.

oneLiner: Confirmed Y-site INCOMPATIBLE list: ciprofloxacin, vancomycin, methylprednisolone, gentamicin, tobramycin, magnesium sulfate (concentrated), calcium chloride, methotrexate, bicarbonate, bretylium.
notes: Trissel-confirmed propofol Y-site incompatibilities (visible oiling / lipid coalescence within minutes at clinical concentrations). All other drugs without a confirmed-compatible Trissel study should be treated as incompatible. Always inspect a shared lumen visually for any oiling.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Compatibility of propofol injectable emulsion with selected drugs during simulated Y-site administration. Am J Health Syst Pharm 1997.

oneLiner: Concentrated magnesium destabilises propofol lipid emulsion at Y-site.
notes: Particularly relevant in pre-eclamptic patients on magnesium who require intubation / sedation. Use separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Calcium chloride destabilises propofol lipid emulsion — separate lumens.
notes: Divalent cations promote droplet coalescence in the propofol emulsion. Use separate lumens; if single-line, pause-flush sequence.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Documented Y-site incompatible — emulsion destabilisation.
notes: Trissel-listed propofol Y-site incompatibility. Separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Documented Y-site incompatible.
notes: Trissel-listed propofol Y-site incompatibility.

references.label: Trissel LA et al. Propofol Y-site compatibility studies.

oneLiner: Bicarbonate is incompatible with the great majority of IV drugs at Y-site (catecholamines, calcium, magnesium, midazolam, morphine, vancomycin, KCl in concentrated mix, most acidic drugs).
notes: Bicarbonate's high pH and the carbonate equilibrium make it incompatible with almost every clinically important co-infusate. Y-site COMPATIBLE list is short: heparin, insulin (limited data — treat as conditional), some chemo agents. Best practice: dedicated lumen for bicarbonate boluses or infusion. In crash scenarios, pause-flush-bicarb-flush-resume on a single line.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Sodium bicarbonate.

oneLiner: Peripheral: ≤ 40 mmol/L concentration, ≤ 10 mmol/h rate. Central: ≤ 100 mmol/L, ≤ 20 mmol/h, on cardiac monitoring.
notes: Bolus IV push of neat KCl is rapidly fatal — never administer as a push. Higher rates than the central cap (e.g. 40 mmol/h) are sometimes used in life-threatening hypokalaemia with continuous ECG monitoring; this is intensivist-led practice with explicit written orders.

references.label: ISMP High-Alert Medications list — concentrated potassium chloride.

oneLiner: Infuse at ≤ 10 mg/min (or ≥ 60 min for a 1 g dose) to avoid red-person syndrome (histamine-mediated flushing, hypotension).
notes: Red-person syndrome is rate-related (not allergic) — it can be prevented by extending the infusion (≥ 60 min for 1 g, ≥ 90 min for 1.5 g, ≥ 120 min for ≥ 2 g) and pre-treatment with H1 antihistamines if there is a prior history.
alternative: Slow the infusion; pre-treat with diphenhydramine if recurrent.

references.label: Vancomycin HCl injection — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: ≤ 50 mg/min adult; reduce to ≤ 25 mg/min in elderly / cardiac patients. Hypotension and arrhythmia at higher rates are propylene glycol mediated.
notes: Faster infusion rates risk hypotension, bradycardia, and ventricular arrhythmia largely attributable to the propylene glycol vehicle (and direct phenytoin myocardial effects). Continuous ECG and BP monitoring during loading.

references.label: Phenytoin sodium injection SmPC.

oneLiner: ≤ 2 mg/mL via peripheral (high phlebitis risk); > 2 mg/mL MUST be central. In-line 0.22 µm filter recommended.
notes: Phlebitis risk is significant even at ≤ 2 mg/mL peripherally — consider central access early for any prolonged infusion. Non-PVC tubing preferred for maintenance.

references.label: Cordarone IV (amiodarone HCl) — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Catecholamine oxidised in alkaline bicarbonate — separate lumens or pause-flush sequence.
notes: Same mechanism as norepinephrine + bicarbonate. Visible browning, loss of inotropy.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dobutamine / Sodium bicarbonate.

oneLiner: Oxidised in alkaline bicarbonate — separate lumens or pause-flush sequence.
notes: Catecholamine oxidation in alkaline media. Visible browning and loss of pressor activity.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dopamine / Sodium bicarbonate.

oneLiner: Oxidised in alkaline bicarbonate — separate lumens.
notes: Same alkaline-incompatibility pattern as other catecholamine-like agents.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Phenylephrine.

oneLiner: Catecholamine oxidation by alkaline furosemide; separate lumens.
notes: Visible discolouration and loss of inotropy. Common pairing in decompensated HF — keep on separate lumens.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dobutamine / Furosemide.

oneLiner: Alkaline furosemide oxidises catecholamine — separate lumens.
notes: Same alkaline-catecholamine incompatibility pattern.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Epinephrine / Furosemide.

oneLiner: Catecholamine oxidation by alkaline furosemide; separate lumens.
notes: Visible discolouration on Y-site contact at clinical concentrations.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Dopamine / Furosemide.

oneLiner: No formal Y-site study — separate lumens preferred.
notes: Trissel does not list a definitive Y-site study. Best practice: keep bicarbonate on a separate lumen.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Vasopressin (limited bicarbonate data).

oneLiner: Midazolam is buffered acidic; alkaline bicarbonate produces visible precipitate at Y-site.
notes: Documented incompatibility. Use a separate lumen for bicarbonate boluses; pause-flush-bicarb-flush-resume on single-line access.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Midazolam.

oneLiner: Already covered in magnesium-calcium — this duplicate flags the bag-mixing scenario: never premix Ca and Mg in a single bag.
notes: Even if Y-site administration is occasionally tolerated at very low concentrations, bag-mixing (additive) of Ca and Mg produces a precipitate at typical replacement concentrations. Compound separately.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Magnesium / Calcium.

oneLiner: Calcium chloride extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis — central administration preferred. Calcium gluconate is the peripheral form of choice.
notes: 10% CaCl₂ is highly hypertonic and irritant. Extravasation can require surgical debridement. Use a central line where feasible; if peripheral is the only option (emergency hyperkalaemia, arrest), use a large vein, dilute when time allows, and inspect the site frequently.

references.label: Calcium chloride 10% injection — manufacturer prescribing information.

oneLiner: Tolerated in the same syringe for procedural sedation. Pharmacodynamic synergy on apnoea is the safety concern, not chemistry.
notes: Common ED / endoscopy practice; observed to be physically stable in the syringe over the short hold time before administration. Titrate slowly and monitor for additive respiratory depression.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Midazolam / Fentanyl.

oneLiner: Stable in the same syringe at the standard ED ketofol ratios (1:1 to 4:1 propofol:ketamine). Use within the hold-time specified by your protocol.
notes: Visually inspect the syringe for any oiling immediately before injection. Common protocol: 5 mg/mL propofol + 5 mg/mL ketamine (1:1 by volume of standard concentrations), titrated in 1-2 mL aliquots. Pharmacodynamic synergy on sedation depth; ketamine offsets propofol's respiratory and haemodynamic suppression.

references.label: Andolfatto G et al. Ketamine-propofol combination (ketofol) for procedural sedation. Ann Emerg Med 2012.

drugB: Compatibility considerations when switching brand / formulation
oneLiner: Generic switches can change the diluent, vehicle, pH and buffer — re-verify compatibility tables when a brand changes.
notes: Different manufacturers use different vehicles (e.g. propofol's lipid composition differs by brand; diazepam's propylene-glycol content varies). When a brand or formulation changes during a shortage, check the new SmPC and the local pharmacy's compatibility table — the previous Y-site profile may not apply.
alternative: Verify the new SmPC; consult local pharmacy.

references.label: ASHP — Drug Shortages and Medication Safety.

oneLiner: Conventional amphotericin B (deoxycholate) precipitates in saline and with most drugs at Y-site — dilute in D5W only, run on dedicated line.
notes: Conventional ampB is a colloidal suspension stabilised by deoxycholate; it aggregates in saline and on contact with most acidic / divalent-cation co-infusates. Use D5W as diluent, dedicated line, in-line filter generally avoided (clogs). Lipid formulations (liposomal, lipid complex) have different but still restrictive compatibility profiles — check each.
alternative: Liposomal amphotericin B has a slightly broader compatibility profile (still dedicate the line). Use D5W diluent.

references.label: Amphotericin B deoxycholate — manufacturer prescribing information.
Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Amphotericin B.

oneLiner: Nafcillin has a narrow Y-site compatibility window — precipitates with many common drugs.
notes: Documented Y-site incompatible: aminoglycosides (inactivation rule), labetalol, midazolam (variable), vancomycin (variable), pantoprazole, ciprofloxacin, hydromorphone (variable). Best practice: dedicated line, NS diluent.

references.label: Trissel's Handbook on Injectable Drugs — Nafcillin.
